title: General Relativity
subject: Relativity
summary: A physical-first introduction to general relativity following Hartle: the equivalence principle, geodesics, the Schwarzschild solution and its tests, black holes, gravitational waves, and cosmology, with the tensor calculus and Einstein equation introduced after the physics is in hand.

units.title: Gravity as geometry
units.summary: The equivalence principle motivates describing gravity as curvature of spacetime; special relativity is reviewed in the language of four-vectors, and the metric becomes the central object.

lessons.title: The equivalence principle and why free fall suggests geometry
objectives: State the weak equivalence principle (gravitational mass equals inertial mass) and the Einstein equivalence principle, and describe an Eotvos-type torsion-balance test.
Explain why universality of free fall suggests that gravity is a property of spacetime (curvature) rather than a force, and why the local inertial frame is only local (tidal effects).

objectives: Raise and lower indices with the Minkowski metric using the summation convention.
Construct the four-velocity u^mu and four-momentum p^mu = (E/c, p) and show p.p = -m^2 c^2.
Explain proper time as the length of a worldline and why a free particle's worldline maximizes proper time (twin paradox).

lessons.title: The metric, line element, and coordinates
objectives: Compute lengths, areas, and volumes from a metric line element, using the 2-sphere ds^2 = R^2(d theta^2 + sin^2 theta d phi^2) as the model example.
Write flat space in polar and spherical coordinates and distinguish coordinate artifacts from invariant geometric facts.

lessons.title: Light cones, local inertial frames, and intrinsic curvature
objectives: Read light cones and coordinate speeds of light from a given metric.
Define a local inertial frame (g_{mu nu} = eta_{mu nu} at a point, first derivatives vanishing) and explain why it exists.
Test for intrinsic curvature with measurable quantities (circumference-to-radius ratio, angle sum of a triangle) rather than from an embedding.

units.title: Geodesics and the Schwarzschild geometry
units.summary: Free fall as geodesic motion; the Schwarzschild solution outside a spherical mass and its observable consequences: redshift, perihelion precession, light bending, and time delay.

lessons.title: The geodesic equation and Christoffel symbols
objectives: Derive the geodesic equation by extremizing proper time with the Euler-Lagrange equations.
Read off the Christoffel symbols from the Euler-Lagrange equations and verify them for flat space in polar coordinates and for the 2-sphere.
demoIdeas: Geodesic shooter: choose a surface or a metric, set initial position and direction, and integrate the geodesic equation, showing parallel-looking paths converge on a sphere.

lessons.title: Conserved quantities, the Newtonian limit, and null geodesics
objectives: Use a cyclic coordinate or Killing vector to find conserved quantities (energy and angular momentum) along a geodesic.
Show that the Newtonian limit of the geodesic equation is d^2x/dt^2 = -grad Phi when g_00 = -(1 + 2 Phi/c^2).
Write the equations of null geodesics for light rays.

lessons.title: The Schwarzschild metric, its coordinates, and gravitational redshift
objectives: Write the Schwarzschild line element and identify r_s = 2GM/c^2; compute r_s for the Earth (about 9 mm) and the Sun (about 3 km).
Interpret the coordinates t and r (areal radius) and distinguish coordinate time from the proper time of a static observer.
Derive the gravitational redshift between static observers at r1 and r2 as the ratio of sqrt(1 - r_s/r) factors.

lessons.title: Conserved quantities and the effective potential for Schwarzschild orbits
objectives: Derive the radial equation (dr/dtau)^2 + V_eff(r) = E^2 from the conserved energy and angular momentum and the normalization of the four-velocity.
Derive the effective potential V_eff = (1 - r_s/r)(1 + L^2/(m^2 c^2 r^2)) and compare it with the Newtonian one, identifying the new attractive term -r_s L^2/(m^2 c^2 r^3).

lectures.title: Lecture 5: Metric for a gravitational field

demoIdeas: Effective-potential plotter for Schwarzschild with sliders for angular momentum and energy, marking circular orbits and the ISCO.

lessons.title: Circular orbits, the ISCO, the photon sphere, and accretion efficiency
objectives: Reduce the radial equation of motion for massive particles to (dr/dtau)^2 + V_eff = E^2 and classify bound, unbound, and plunging orbits.
Locate circular orbits, the innermost stable circular orbit at r = 6GM/c^2, and the photon sphere at r = 3GM/c^2.
Compute the binding energy released at the ISCO and relate it to accretion efficiency (about 5.7%).
demoIdeas: Orbit-type map: slide the radius from 1.5 r_s outward and color circular orbits as stable, unstable, or absent, marking the photon sphere at 3GM/c^2 and the ISCO at 6GM/c^2.

lessons.title: Perihelion precession and Mercury's 43 arcseconds
objectives: Explain why the Newtonian inverse-square law gives closed orbits and how a small 1/r^3 correction to the orbit equation makes the ellipse rotate.
Derive the perihelion advance Delta phi = 6 pi G M / (c^2 a (1 - e^2)) per orbit by perturbation of the Newtonian orbit and compute about 43 arcseconds per century for Mercury.

lessons.title: Light deflection and the Shapiro time delay
objectives: Derive the deflection of light by a mass, Delta phi = 4GM/(c^2 b), and compute 1.75 arcseconds for starlight grazing the Sun.
Compute the Shapiro time delay for a radar signal passing near the Sun.

units.title: Black holes
units.summary: The Schwarzschild horizon, collapse, Kruskal extension, astrophysical black holes, Hawking radiation, and the Kerr geometry.

lessons.title: Coordinate singularities, radial infall, and the event horizon
objectives: Show that r = r_s is a coordinate singularity (finite curvature invariants) while r = 0 is a true singularity.
Compute the proper time for radial infall to the singularity (finite) and the coordinate time to the horizon (infinite).
Use Eddington-Finkelstein coordinates to show light cones tilt inward and define the event horizon.

objectives: Describe the Kruskal-Szekeres maximal extension and why the Einstein-Rosen bridge is not traversable.
Explain tidal stretching ('spaghettification') and compute its size for a given black-hole mass.

lessons.title: Evidence for black holes and the Hawking temperature
objectives: Summarize the evidence for stellar-mass black holes in X-ray binaries and a supermassive black hole at the Galactic center.
Derive or quote the Hawking temperature T_H = hbar c^3 / (8 pi G M k_B) and compute it for a solar-mass hole (about 62 nK).

units.title: Tensors and curvature
units.summary: The mathematics of general relativity: tensors, the covariant derivative, parallel transport, and the Riemann, Ricci, and Einstein tensors.

lessons.title: Vectors, dual vectors, and tensor transformation laws
objectives: Define vectors as tangent vectors to curves and dual vectors as linear maps, and write their transformation laws under coordinate changes.
Construct and transform (m,n) tensors, and test whether a given set of components transforms as a tensor.

lessons.title: Index gymnastics, the metric, and why partial derivatives fail
objectives: Raise and lower indices with the metric and form scalars by contraction.
Show that the partial derivative of a vector field is not a tensor.

lectures.title: Lecture 3: Tensors Continued (index gymnastics and contraction)

lessons.title: The covariant derivative and the Christoffel formula
objectives: Define the covariant derivative nabla_mu V^nu = partial_mu V^nu + Gamma^nu_{mu lambda} V^lambda and show how Gamma transforms.
Derive the Christoffel formula from metric compatibility and the absence of torsion.

lessons.title: Parallel transport, holonomy, and geodesics as straightest lines

lessons.title: Tidal forces and the equation of geodesic deviation
objectives: Derive the geodesic deviation equation and identify the tidal tensor with the Riemann tensor.
Relate the Riemann tensor in the Newtonian limit to the tidal tensor partial_i partial_j Phi.

lessons.title: The Riemann tensor: definition, components, and symmetries
objectives: Define the Riemann tensor through the commutator of covariant derivatives and compute its components for the 2-sphere.
List the symmetries of the Riemann tensor and count its 20 independent components in four dimensions.
demoIdeas: Commutator loop: transport a vector around a small rectangle on a sphere with sliders for the loop's size and latitude, displaying the rotation angle and its match to R times the enclosed area.

lessons.title: The Ricci tensor, Ricci scalar, and curvature in vacuum
objectives: Contract the Riemann tensor to obtain the Ricci tensor and Ricci scalar and compute them for the 2-sphere.
Explain why R_{mu nu} = 0 (vacuum) does not imply flat spacetime.

lessons.title: The Bianchi identity and the Einstein tensor
objectives: State the contracted Bianchi identity nabla_mu G^{mu nu} = 0 and explain its consequence.
Construct the Einstein tensor G = R - (1/2) R g and argue why it is the natural divergence-free tensor of second order in derivatives.

lessons.title: The stress-energy tensor and its conservation
objectives: Write the stress-energy tensor for dust and a perfect fluid, and state energy-momentum conservation nabla_mu T^{mu nu} = 0.
Compute components of T^{mu nu} in a fluid rest frame and in a boosted frame.
